diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The coding workload appears to be CPU-throttled inside the container: python3 sustains almost exactly 0.25 CPU-seconds per wall-second for about 12 seconds, then stops abruptly. This looks like a per-container CPU quota rather than host-wide CPU saturation; the trace does not expose throttled-seconds directly, so the quota attribution is an inference, not a directly recorded counter.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared scheduled-runtime payloads in successive two-second windows from 03:17:26.200 through 03:17:58.200. python3 rises to 479.8 ms/2s at 03:17:42.200–44.200 and remains near 250 ms/s through 03:17:52.200–54.200 (per-window totals 249.7–257.7 ms/s; python3 has 89–96% of measured runtime). At 03:17:54.200–56.200 total runtime falls to 19.3 ms/s and python3 is no longer a leading consumer. The trace shows four CPUs idling during low-activity periods, not host saturation; sampled block issue/completion counts do not show sustained outstanding I/O, and paired wakeup checks do not establish general run-queue starvation. Raw scheduling lines identify python3 as an active workload, but the workers found no direct throttling counter, so the sustained near-250 ms/s ceiling is the decisive circumstantial evidence.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The lower boundary is where scheduled runtime changes from roughly 138 ms/s in 03:17:40.200–42.200 to 255 ms/s in 03:17:42.200–44.200 and then remains near 250 ms/s across six consecutive two-second windows. The upper boundary is the sharp drop at 03:17:54.200: total runtime falls to 19.3 ms/s in the next window and python3 is no longer among the leading consumers.
